Background of Machined Surfaces The measurement and analysis of machined surfaces have evolved significantly over the decades, driven by the need for greater precision and understanding of surface characteristics. Initially, touch-based methods were the go-to, where probes delicately interacted with the surface to measure roughness [1,2]. These methods were limited in their precision and ability to capture detailed surface features, necessitating a transition to more advanced techniques. As the demand for higher accuracy grew, more advanced techniques were developed. Hydraulic and pneumatic methods emerged, offering better control and more precise measurements [3,4]. These advancements marked a noteworthy improvement but still faced limitations in capturing the full complexity of machined surfaces [5,6]. The development of optical reflection techniques represented a major leap forward. These methods allowed for non-contact measurements, significantly reducing errors and providing higher-resolution data [7,8]. Instruments such as tracker-tip devices enhanced the ability to measure surface roughness with great precision by magnifying surface vibrations [9,10,11]. These instruments demonstrated the integration of mechanical, pneumatic, electronic, and optical technologies, emphasizing the multidisciplinary nature of advancements in surface measurement. The machining field has evolved to include image processing techniques that provide detailed, real-time analysis of surface characteristics. This evolution highlights the ongoing development toward precision and a deeper understanding of the study of machined surfaces. 1.2. The importance of evaluating surfaces becomes clear when considering the negative effects, such as defects or inconsistencies on machined surfaces [12,13]. Even the slightest imperfection can propagate into severe complications, possibly leading to catastrophic failure of components and machine systems. This crucial interrelation between surface quality and component functionality renders surface evaluation a paramount concern in manufacturing disciplines [14]. Surface evaluation, with its wide range of applications, is not confined to laboratory investigations, particularly in the realm of metals and plastics [15,16]. fetched_contents.text: Automatic Identification of Tool Wear Based on Convolutional Neural Network in Face Milling Process Abstract Monitoring of tool wear in machining process has found its importance to predict tool life, reduce equipment downtime, and tool costs. Traditional visual methods require expert experience and human resources to obtain accurate tool wear information. With the development of charge-coupled device (CCD) image sensor and the deep learning algorithms, it has become possible to use the convolutional neural network (CNN) model to automatically identify the wear types of high-temperature alloy tools in the face milling process. In this paper, the CNN model is developed based on our image dataset. The convolutional automatic encoder (CAE) is used to pre-train the network model, and the model parameters are fine-tuned by back propagation (BP) algorithm combined with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm. The established ToolWearnet network model has the function of identifying the tool wear types. The experimental results show that the average recognition precision rate of the model can reach 96.20%. At the same time, the automatic detection algorithm of tool wear value is improved by combining the identified tool wear types. In order to verify the feasibility of the method, an experimental system is built on the machine tool. By matching the frame rate of the industrial camera and the machine tool spindle speed, the wear image information of all the inserts can be obtained in the machining gap. The automatic detection method of tool wear value is compared with the result of manual detection by high precision digital optical microscope, the mean absolute percentage error is 4.76%, which effectively verifies the effectiveness and practicality of the method. Keywords: tool wear monitoring, superalloy tool, convolutional neural network, image recognition 1. Introduction of Tool Condition Monitoring (TCM) In milling operations, the quality of machined workpiece is highly dependent on the state of the cutting insert. Factors such as wear, corrosion, or fatigue can affect tool wear. Therefore, monitoring of tool wear in machining process has found its importance to predict tool life, reduce equipment downtime, and optimize machining parameters [1]. The detection method of tool wear can be categorized into two groups: direct and indirect method [2]. Indirect measurement is the use of sensors to measure a signal related to tool wear and obtained by analyzing the signal. Applicable signals that are widely used for tool wear measurement include acoustic emission, force, vibration, current, and power signals, etc. For example, Yao et al. [3] used the acoustic emission signal, the spindle motor current signal, and the feed motor current signal to monitor the tool wear state. Li et al. [4] used acoustic emission (AE) signals to realize the TCM and tool life prediction. Jauregui et al. [5] used cutting force and vibration signals to monitor tool wear state in the high-speed micro-milling process. Prasad et al. [6] analyzed the sound and light-emitting signals during milling and obtained the relationship between tool wear and surface roughness. However, all of these signals are heavily contaminated by the inherent noise in the industrial environment, reducing their performance [7]. Recent advances in digital image processing have suggested the machine vision should be used for TCM. In this case, the direct method of measuring tool wear has higher accuracy and reliability than the indirect method [7]. An unsupervised classification was used to segment the tool wear area through an artificial neural network (ANN) and then used to predict tool wear life [8]. Garcia-Ordas et al. [9] used computer vision technology to extract the shape descriptor of the tool wear area, combined with the machine learning model to achieve TCM. D’Addona et al. [10] used ANN and DNA-based computing, the tool wear degree was predicted based on image information extracted from the pre-processing. Alegre-Gutierrez et al. [7] proposed a method based on image texture analysis for TCM in the edge contour milling. The extracted descriptor of the tool wear area and the cutting parameters as the input parameters of wavelet neural network (WNN) model, which can predict the tool wear degree [11]. Mikolajczyk et al. [12] developed a system that can automatically measure the wear degree of the cutting edge by analyzing its image. Therefore, applying machine vision method in TCM has become more and more mature. Since deep learning is a network structure with multiple layers of nonlinear series processing units, it is possible to omit data preprocessing and use the original data for model training and testing directly [13]. With deep learning method, enormous breakthroughs have been made in image recognition and classification [14,15,16], fault diagnosis [17,18], and medical health [19,20], etc., and CNN has become one of the research focuses in artificial intelligence algorithm directions. In the mechanical manufacturing industry, CNN can be used for monitoring the operating conditions of gearboxes, bearings, etc., to identify the faults intelligently and classify the diagnosis [21,22,23]. In the aspect of TCM, Fatemeh et al. [24] used extracted features to train and test the Bayesian network, support vector machine, K nearest neighbor regression model, and established CNN model. The experimental results show that the CNN model has a higher recognition rate precision for TCM. Zhang et al. [25] converted the original vibration signal into an energy spectrum map by wavelet packet transform, which trained and tested the energy spectrum map based on the CNN to classify the tool wear. Image-processing features can quantify tool wear by capturing both structural and textural changes that correlate with wear progression. The most informative features for wear detection are edges, roughness, cracks, and morphology, because these characteristics reflect the physical degradation of the tool surface. In the reviewed machining literature, image processing is used for surface roughness assessment, defect detection, and tool wear analysis, with emphasis on the ability to capture detailed surface features [N1-F1]. A dedicated tool-wear image-processing paper also states that tool-wear images are acquired by a camera and that wear boundaries are recognized by image preprocessing, threshold segmentation, and edge detection [N1-R4]. This workflow indicates that edges are used to identify wear boundaries, while segmentation and preprocessing help isolate wear-relevant regions from the broader image.

Cracks and morphology are similarly important because tool wear often manifests as localized damage, edge blunting, flank wear, or surface irregularities. The review notes that image processing techniques are applied for tool wear analysis, surface roughness assessment, and defect detection, which implies that crack-like features and irregular surface morphology are treated as meaningful wear indicators [N1-R3]. The image-based tool-wear benchmark study further shows that CNN-based image analysis can be used to automatically identify wear types and even estimate wear values from processed images, supporting the idea that wear severity can be inferred from image texture and shape descriptors [N3-F2]. A separate tool-wear classification paper also mentions that CNN models extract wear characteristics from tool-wear images, reinforcing that feature extraction is not limited to edges alone [N3-R2].

Mapping image features to specific wear states or severity levels requires linking observable image patterns to measurable wear quantities. The literature suggests that image features are extracted from tool-wear images and used as inputs for classification or regression models [N3-R2][N3-F2]. In the reviewed CNN-based method, high-resolution images are used directly to predict wear levels, which implies a direct mapping from image features to wear severity rather than just presence/absence [N3-R1]. The same source also states that the model can estimate wear values by combining identified wear types with quantitative image analysis, showing that severity estimation is often a multi-step process: first classify wear state, then estimate magnitude from associated image features [N3-F2]. A broader review of image processing methods for surface and tool condition assessments notes that image processing helps refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness and reveals intricate details of machined surfaces, which is relevant to mapping roughness and morphology changes to wear states [N1-F1].

Preprocessing and normalization steps are critical for improving feature extraction reliability. The image-based tool-wear paper explicitly states that wear characteristics are extracted from tool-wear images after image size normalization [N3-R2]. Another study uses an MV system with an automated feature-based image registration strategy to spatially align tool-wear images, indicating that alignment is a key preprocessing step to ensure consistent feature extraction across images [N3-R3]. The same review notes that image processing techniques are applied to machined surfaces and tool conditions, emphasizing that preprocessing helps reduce noise and capture more accurate surface details [N1-F1]. The CNN-based tool-wear study also uses pre-training and fine-tuning with backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent, which suggests that normalization and feature normalization are part of the training pipeline to improve model stability [N3-F2]. Together, these sources support a workflow in which normalization, segmentation, edge detection, and alignment are used to make image features more reliable and comparable across samples [N1-R4][N3-R2][N3-R3].

The reviewed CNN-based tool-wear study explicitly mentions that images are processed after normalization and that preprocessing is used to extract wear characteristics [N3-R2]. It also states that tool-wear images are acquired by a camera, which implies that lighting and camera setup can influence the quality of the input images [N1-R4]. The review of image processing for surface and tool condition assessments notes that image processing helps refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness and reveals intricate details, but it also implies that poor image quality can reduce the ability to capture those details accurately [N1-F1]. In industrial settings, motion blur and inconsistent lighting can further degrade wear visibility, making edge detection and crack detection less reliable.

Tool types and wear modes influence image-processing performance because different tools have different wear signatures and surface geometries. The literature explicitly references turning, milling, and drilling contexts, showing that wear analysis must account for the machining mode [N1-F1][N1-R3]. A dedicated tool-wear image-processing paper states that tool-wear images are acquired by a camera and that wear boundaries are recognized by image preprocessing, threshold segmentation, and edge detection [N1-R4], which suggests that tools with complex flank geometries may require more sophisticated segmentation. The same paper also notes that the objective is to determine the state of tool wear in a flexible manufacturing system, implying that tool geometry and wear mode must be matched to the image-processing pipeline [N3-R4]. The CNN-based study further shows that image preprocessing and normalization are needed to extract wear characteristics, reinforcing that tool-specific preprocessing is important when wear modes differ [N3-R2].

Industrial deployment involves tradeoffs between accuracy, speed, and feasibility. The reviewed benchmark study reports high accuracy and F1 scores for multi-dataset tool-wear detection, but it also notes that dataset balance and preprocessing strategies are critical challenges [N4-F3]. This implies that high accuracy is difficult to achieve unless the data are balanced and the model is trained on representative samples. The multi-dataset benchmark also highlights the need for standardized pipelines and transfer learning to adapt models from laboratory data to industrial environments, which is a major practical constraint for deployment [N4-F3]. Overall, image-based characterization is most effective when image quality, lighting, and motion are controlled, and when the model is tuned to the specific tool type and wear mode rather than assuming a universal solution [N3-R2][N1-R4][N4-F3].

Tool-wear severity and multi-level classification are handled in practice by distinguishing wear stages from one another using progressively more severe image features. The reviewed literature identifies wear stages such as initial wear (IW), steady-state wear (SSW), and accelerated wear (AW) as the stages that define the total lifespan of a tool [N2-R2]. This stage-based framing means that severity is not treated as a single binary outcome but as a sequence of progressively worse conditions, where mild wear corresponds to early-stage or low-magnitude degradation, moderate wear corresponds to steady-state wear, and severe wear corresponds to accelerated wear or near-end-of-life conditions [N2-R2]. The CNN-based tool-wear classification paper also reports an accuracy of more than 93% for wear classification, showing that multi-class classification is feasible and can capture these distinctions [N5-R2]. Another study reports that a CNN model achieves an accuracy of more than 93% in all tested scenarios, further supporting the use of multi-level classification [N5-R2].

Multi-level classification differs from binary wear detection in that it explicitly partitions wear states into multiple severity classes, rather than merely distinguishing “worn” from “not worn.” The reviewed CNN-based tool-wear system explicitly states that the network is used to identify wear types and that the automatic detection algorithm improves wear value estimation by combining identified wear types [N3-F2]. This indicates that multi-level classification is a richer task than simple binary classification, because it requires the model to recognize not only whether wear exists, but also how severe it is. The review of image processing for surface and tool condition assessments also notes that image processing can refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness and reveal intricate details of machined surfaces, which is important for severity estimation because roughness and morphology change nonlinearly with wear progression [N1-F1]. In contrast, binary wear detection is limited to presence/absence and may miss the full severity spectrum [N1-R3][N3-F2].

Uncertainty and measurement noise affect severity estimation because image features can be ambiguous, especially when wear is still mild or when noise interferes with segmentation and edge detection. The CNN-based tool-wear benchmark reports high recognition precision but also indicates that the automatic detection algorithm has a mean absolute percentage error of 4.76%, showing that noise can reduce the accuracy of severity estimates [N3-F2]. The multi-dataset benchmark study also emphasizes that dataset balance and preprocessing strategies are critical challenges, suggesting that imbalance or noisy preprocessing can inflate false positives or false negatives in multi-class wear classification [N4-F3]. Furthermore, the review notes that image processing helps refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness, which implies that small changes in roughness can be meaningful for mild wear but harder to distinguish from measurement noise [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that severity estimation should be interpreted cautiously when the image is noisy, the tool is in a transitional wear state, or the dataset is imbalanced [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Tool-wear severity and multi-level classification are handled in practice by distinguishing wear stages from one another using progressively more severe image features. ## How image processing can be effectively applied to characterize tool wear

Image processing is effective for characterizing tool wear because it translates physical surface degradation into measurable image features that can be analyzed automatically. The core idea is to capture structural and textural changes that correlate with wear progression, such as edges, roughness, cracks, and morphology [N1-F1][N1-R4][N1-R3]. These features are particularly useful because tool wear often manifests as localized damage, edge blunting, flank wear, or surface irregularities, which image-processing techniques are well suited to detect [N3-F2]. The literature also shows that tool-wear images are acquired by a camera and that wear boundaries are recognized by image preprocessing, threshold segmentation, and edge detection, indicating that edges and segmentation are central to the workflow [N1-R4]. In practice, this means image processing is not just about inspecting an image; it is about isolating wear-relevant regions and extracting the visual signatures that indicate wear severity [N1-R4][N3-R2].

### 1) What image features are most informative for wear detection?

The most informative features for wear detection are:

- **Edges**: Used to identify wear boundaries and locate regions of interest [N1-R4].
- **Roughness**: Image processing is applied to refine surface roughness measurement mechanisms and reveal intricate surface details, making roughness a key indicator of wear [N1-F1].
- **Cracks and morphology**: Tool-wear analysis, defect detection, and surface roughness assessment all imply that crack-like features and irregular surface morphology are meaningful wear indicators [N1-R3][N1-F1].
- **Shape descriptors and texture**: CNN-based methods extract wear characteristics from tool-wear images and can automatically identify wear types and estimate wear values, showing that texture and shape are used to infer wear state [N3-F2][N3-R2].

These features are especially useful because they are directly tied to the physical degradation of the tool. For example, as tool wear progresses, surface roughness increases, morphology becomes more irregular, and cracks or blunting become visible [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### 2) How to map image features to specific wear states or severity levels

Mapping image features to specific wear states or severity levels requires linking observable patterns to measurable wear quantities. The literature shows that image features are extracted from tool-wear images and used as inputs for classification or regression models [N3-R2][N3-F2]. In one CNN-based method, high-resolution images are used directly to predict wear levels, which implies a direct mapping from image features to wear severity rather than just presence/absence [N3-R1]. The same study also states that the model can estimate wear values by combining identified wear types with quantitative image analysis, showing that severity estimation is often a multi-step process: first classify wear state, then estimate magnitude from associated image features [N3-F2].

In practice, this means image-based wear characterization is often multi-level rather than binary. The reviewed literature identifies wear stages such as initial wear (IW), steady-state wear (SSW), and accelerated wear (AW) as the stages that define the total lifespan of a tool [N2-R2]. This stage-based framework supports the idea that mild, moderate, and severe wear can be distinguished by progressively more severe image features [N2-R2]. The CNN-based tool-wear classification paper also reports an accuracy of more than 93% for wear classification, showing that multi-class classification is feasible and can capture these distinctions [N5-R2].

### 3) What preprocessing and normalization steps improve feature extraction reliability

Preprocessing and normalization are critical for making image features reliable and comparable across samples. The image-based tool-wear study explicitly states that wear characteristics are extracted from tool-wear images after image size normalization [N3-R2]. Another study uses an MV system with an automated feature-based image registration strategy to spatially align tool-wear images, indicating that alignment is a key preprocessing step to ensure consistent feature extraction [N3-R3]. The review of image processing for surface and tool condition assessments notes that image processing helps refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness and reveals intricate details, which implies that preprocessing helps reduce noise and capture more accurate surface details [N1-F1].

In addition, the CNN-based tool-wear study uses pre-training and fine-tuning with backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent, which suggests that normalization and feature normalization are part of the training pipeline to improve model stability [N3-F2]. Together, these sources support a workflow in which normalization, segmentation, edge detection, and alignment are used to make image features more reliable and comparable across samples [N1-R4][N3-R2][N3-R3].

### 4) Which model architectures are suitable for tool-wear images?

For tool-wear classification, CNNs are especially appropriate because they are designed to automatically extract hierarchical features from images, making them well suited for wear-state recognition [N3-F2]. The reviewed literature explicitly states that CNNs are used for tool wear monitoring and that CNN-based models can automatically identify wear types and estimate wear values [N3-F2]. A separate study reports that a CNN model achieves an accuracy of more than 93% in all tested scenarios, demonstrating strong practical performance [N5-R2]. The multi-dataset benchmark study also notes that CNN-based classification of wear mechanisms from SEM images achieved 73% test accuracy, reinforcing that CNNs are a standard architecture for this task [N4-F3].

Transfer learning is also relevant because the benchmark study states that transfer learning has been shown effective for adapting models trained on laboratory data to industrial machines [N4-F3]. This is important when there is a gap between controlled training data and noisy industrial images, because transfer learning can improve generalization to real-world conditions.

### 5) How to split data, balance classes, and avoid overfitting

Splitting data, balancing classes, and avoiding overfitting are central to building reliable wear classifiers. The multi-dataset benchmark study reports that the best model achieved 0.972 (+/-0.008) accuracy and 0.97 F1-score on 5-fold cross-validation, showing that cross-validation is a standard way to assess generalization [N4-R1]. It also emphasizes dataset balance and magnification consistency as critical challenges, indicating that class imbalance or inconsistent image preprocessing can degrade performance [N4-F3].

The reviewed CNN-based tool-wear study uses pre-training and fine-tuning with backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent, which are standard ways to avoid overfitting when the dataset is small [N3-F2]. The tool-wear classification paper also notes that the CNN model is developed based on an image dataset, and that preprocessing is used to extract wear characteristics, implying that a well-balanced and preprocessed dataset is essential for model training [N3-R2]. In addition, the benchmark study compares models across different sensor modalities and preprocessing strategies, showing that careful data splitting and preprocessing are necessary to prevent overfitting to specific conditions [N4-F3].

### 6) Which validation metrics are most meaningful for wear-state prediction?

For multi-class classification, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score are all important, but the benchmark study also notes that F1-score balances precision and recall through their harmonic mean, making it a useful default metric for class-imbalanced problems [N4-R2]. The same study mentions AUC-ROC as a metric that evaluates the model’s ranking ability across all possible thresholds, which is especially relevant for industrial monitoring where threshold selection matters [N4-R2]. The benchmarking guide further states that sensitivity and specificity are useful tools for benchmarking performance, and that precision and recall should be used when the goal is to detect rare events or minimize false negatives [N4-R4]. The multi-class classification guide also explains how to apply these metrics in multi-class settings, reinforcing that they should not be used interchangeably [N4-R5].

In practice, the combination of cross-validation, F1-score, and precision/recall provides the most informative evaluation for wear-state prediction, especially when the dataset is imbalanced or the model must be deployed in an industrial setting [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5].

### 7) Practical considerations and limitations

Image-based tool-wear characterization is highly sensitive to image quality, lighting, and tool motion, which can distort feature extraction and classification. The reviewed CNN-based tool-wear study explicitly mentions that images are processed after normalization and that preprocessing is used to extract wear characteristics [N3-R2]. It also states that tool-wear images are acquired by a camera, which implies that lighting and camera setup can influence the quality of the input images [N1-R4]. The review of image processing for surface and tool condition assessments notes that image processing helps refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness and reveals intricate details, but it also implies that poor image quality can reduce the ability to capture those details accurately [N1-F1]. In industrial settings, motion blur and inconsistent lighting can further degrade wear visibility, making edge detection and crack detection less reliable [N3-R2][N1-F1].

Tool types and wear modes influence image-processing performance because different tools have different wear signatures and surface geometries. The literature explicitly references turning, milling, and drilling contexts, showing that wear analysis must account for the machining mode [N1-F1][N1-R3]. A dedicated tool-wear image-processing paper states that tool-wear images are acquired by a camera and that wear boundaries are recognized by image preprocessing, threshold segmentation, and edge detection [N1-R4], which suggests that tools with complex flank geometries may require more sophisticated segmentation. The same paper also notes that the objective is to determine the state of tool wear in a flexible manufacturing system, implying that tool geometry and wear mode must be matched to the image-processing pipeline [N3-R4]. The CNN-based study further shows that image preprocessing and normalization are needed to extract wear characteristics, reinforcing that tool-specific preprocessing is important when wear modes differ [N3-R2].

Industrial deployment involves tradeoffs between accuracy, speed, and feasibility. The reviewed benchmark study reports high accuracy and F1 scores for multi-dataset tool-wear detection, but it also notes that dataset balance and preprocessing strategies are critical challenges [N4-F3]. This implies that high accuracy is difficult to achieve unless the data are balanced and the model is trained on representative samples. The CNN-based tool-wear system is described as an easy-to-use image-based system built with inexpensive components, which suggests that deployment feasibility can be improved by simplifying hardware and software [N2-R1]. At the same time, the study on CNN-based tool wear monitoring in face milling reports that the model achieves 96.20% average recognition precision and that the automatic detection algorithm has a mean absolute percentage error of 4.76%, demonstrating that accuracy can be strong but not perfect [N3-F2]. The multi-dataset benchmark also highlights the need for standardized pipelines and transfer learning to adapt models from laboratory data to industrial environments, which is a major practical constraint for deployment [N4-F3].

### 8) How to handle tool-wear severity and multi-level classification

Tool-wear severity and multi-level classification are handled in practice by distinguishing wear stages from one another using progressively more severe image features. The reviewed literature identifies wear stages such as initial wear (IW), steady-state wear (SSW), and accelerated wear (AW) as the stages that define the total lifespan of a tool [N2-R2]. This stage-based framing means that severity is not treated as a single binary outcome but as a sequence of progressively worse conditions, where mild wear corresponds to early-stage or low-magnitude degradation, moderate wear corresponds to steady-state wear, and severe wear corresponds to accelerated wear or near-end-of-life conditions [N2-R2]. The CNN-based tool-wear classification paper also reports an accuracy of more than 93% for wear classification, showing that multi-class classification is feasible and can capture these distinctions [N5-R2].

Multi-level classification differs from binary wear detection in that it explicitly partitions wear states into multiple severity classes, rather than merely distinguishing “worn” from “not worn.” The reviewed CNN-based tool-wear system explicitly states that the network is used to identify wear types and that the automatic detection algorithm improves wear value estimation by combining identified wear types [N3-F2]. This indicates that multi-level classification is a richer task than simple binary classification, because it requires the model to recognize not only whether wear exists, but also how severe it is. The review of image processing for surface and tool condition assessments also notes that image processing can refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness and reveal intricate details of machined surfaces, which is important for severity estimation because roughness and morphology change nonlinearly with wear progression [N1-F1]. In contrast, binary wear detection is limited to presence/absence and may miss the full severity spectrum [N1-R3][N3-F2].

Uncertainty and measurement noise affect severity estimation because image features can be ambiguous, especially when wear is still mild or when noise interferes with segmentation and edge detection. The CNN-based tool-wear benchmark reports high recognition precision but also indicates that the automatic detection algorithm has a mean absolute percentage error of 4.76%, showing that noise can reduce the accuracy of severity estimates [N3-F2]. The multi-dataset benchmark study also emphasizes that dataset balance and preprocessing strategies are critical challenges, suggesting that imbalance or noisy preprocessing can inflate false positives or false negatives in multi-class wear classification [N4-F3]. Furthermore, the review notes that image processing helps refine mechanisms for measuring surface roughness, which implies that small changes in roughness can be meaningful for mild wear but harder to distinguish from measurement noise [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that severity estimation should be interpreted cautiously when the image is noisy, the tool is in a transitional wear state, or the dataset is imbalanced [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### 9) Overall conclusion

In summary, image processing can be effectively applied to characterize tool wear by combining **feature extraction** with **machine learning**, **preprocessing**, and **careful validation**. The most informative features are edges, roughness, cracks, and morphology [N1-F1][N1-R4][N1-R3]. These features are mapped to wear states or severity levels through classification and regression pipelines, often using CNNs and transfer learning [N3-F2][N5-R2][N4-F3]. Preprocessing and normalization improve feature extraction reliability by normalizing image size, aligning tool-wear images, and reducing noise [N3-R2][N3-R3][N1-F1]. Validation is best supported by cross-validation, F1-score, precision, recall, and AUC-ROC, especially for class-imbalanced or industrial datasets [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5].

However, image-based tool-wear characterization is limited by image quality, lighting, tool motion, and tool-specific wear modes [N3-R2][N1-F1][N1-R4]. Deployment also requires balancing accuracy, speed, and feasibility, and multi-level classification should be treated as a richer task than binary wear detection because it captures the full severity spectrum [N2-R2][N5-R2][N3-F2]. For these reasons, image processing is most effective when it is part of a larger system that includes preprocessing, robust modeling, and careful evaluation in the industrial context [N3-R2][N4-F3][N2-R1].
